title: Addressing & Subnetting
sub: Read any IP, mask, MAC or routing-table line and do the subnet maths in your head and in Python
goals: Convert between dotted decimal, binary, hex and prefix-length forms of an address and a mask
Compute network, broadcast, first, last and usable hosts with the magic-number method
Split a block with VLSM and summarize several blocks into one route
Predict which routing-table entry wins using longest-prefix match
Read IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses and the netmask that macOS prints in hex
Build ipcalc.py, a subnet calculator in pure maths and with the ipaddress module

blocks.text: Every device on a network has to answer two questions before it can send anything: *is the destination on my own network, or must I hand the packet to a router?* and *which router?* Both answers come from arithmetic on addresses and masks, done in binary, by every host and every router, for every packet. In this chapter you will learn that arithmetic well enough to do it on paper, then let Python do it for you and check your work. You will end with a working subnet calculator.

Open Terminal and run `ifconfig en0 | grep 'inet '`. You will see something like `inet 192.168.1.23 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 192.168.1.255`. By the end of this chapter you will be able to say, from that one line, how many hosts the network holds, what its first and last usable addresses are, and why `broadcast` is what it is.
Binary arithmetic for networking

An IPv4 address is a single **32-bit number**. People write it as four 8-bit pieces called **octets**, each shown in decimal (0 to 255), separated by dots. The dots are only for humans; the network sees 32 bits.
Each bit position has a value that doubles as you move left. You need these eight numbers by heart:

blocks.code:
bit position:   7     6     5     4     3     2     1     0
 value:        128    64    32    16     8     4     2     1

blocks.text: To convert a decimal octet to binary, write 1 under every value you take and 0 under the rest. `192 = 128 + 64`, so `11000000`. `168 = 128 + 32 + 8`, so `10101000`. Going the other way, add up the values under each 1. Python does the same job in one line, and the `:08b` format spec pads to 8 bits with zeros:
Try the same conversions interactively with the converter. Toggle bits and watch the decimal and hex change.
Masks are runs of ones

A **subnet mask** is a 32-bit number made of a block of 1s followed by 0s. The 1s mark the **network part** of an address and the 0s mark the **host part**. The only legal octet values in a mask are these, because each one is "some number of 1s, then 0s":
The right-hand column is the **block size** (or "magic number") you will use in a moment. Write it as 256 minus the mask octet.
The one operation that matters: AND

To find which network an address belongs to, a host or router performs a **bitwise AND** of the address with the mask. The result keeps the address bits wherever the mask has a 1 and zeroes everything else:

The network address is the AND. The **broadcast address** is the network address with every host bit set to 1, which is the same as OR-ing the address with the *inverted* mask. Here is the whole calculation in Python, using shifts to pack four octets into one 32-bit integer:

blocks.code:
def to_int(dotted):
    a, b, c, d = (int(x) for x in dotted.split("."))
    return a << 24 | b << 16 | c << 8 | d

def to_dotted(n):
    return ".".join(str((n >> shift) & 255) for shift in (24, 16, 8, 0))

ip = to_int("192.168.1.23")
mask = to_int("255.255.255.192")
wildcard = ~mask & 0xFFFFFFFF          # invert, keep 32 bits
print("network  ", to_dotted(ip & mask))
print("wildcard ", to_dotted(wildcard))
print("broadcast", to_dotted(ip | wildcard))

blocks.text: The inverted mask is called the **wildcard mask**. You will meet it in router access lists and OSPF configuration, where `0.0.0.63` means "the last 6 bits may be anything".
IPv4 anatomy and a little history
An IPv4 address has two parts: a **network prefix** shared by every device on the same network, and a **host identifier** unique within it. Where the line falls depends only on the mask.

In the 1980s the line was fixed by the first bits of the address: **classful addressing** gave Class A (`0...`, /8), Class B (`10...`, /16) and Class C (`110...`, /24) networks. That wasted addresses badly, because an organization needing 300 hosts had to take a 65,534-host Class B. Since 1993 the line can fall on any bit, a scheme called **CIDR** (Classless Inter-Domain Routing, pronounced "cider"). You will still hear "Class C" used loosely for a /24, and some tools print it, but routers ignore classes entirely.
CIDR notation and the four spellings of a mask

CIDR writes a network as an address, a slash and the **prefix length**: the number of leading 1 bits in the mask. `192.168.1.0/24` means "the first 24 bits are the network". The same mask appears in four spellings, and you will meet all four:

tokens.exp: network address: host bits are all zero
separator between address and prefix length
prefix length: the first 26 bits are the network part

blocks.text: Each hex digit is four bits, so `0xffffffc0` is `ff ff ff c0`, which is three full octets of 1s plus `c0 = 11000000`: 24 + 2 = 26 bits. Count the `f`s (four bits each), then add the partial digit using the table above: `e` is 3 bits, `c` is 2, `8` is 1, `0` is 0, and `f` is 4.

blocks.code:
$ ifconfig en0 | grep 'inet '
	inet 192.168.1.23 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 192.168.1.255
$ ifconfig en0 | awk '/inet /{ m=substr($4,3); n=0; for(i=1;i<=length(m);i++){c=substr(m,i,1); n+=(c=="f")*4+(c=="e")*3+(c=="c")*2+(c=="8")*1 } print $2 "/" n }'
192.168.1.23/24

blocks.text: The `awk` program strips the leading `0x` with `substr($4,3)`, walks the hex digits and adds 4 for each `f`, 3 for `e`, and so on. It prints your address with its prefix length. That one-liner is the seed of the "subnet from IP and mask" recipe in [Seeing your own network](#net-local).

blocks.title: Reading the inet line from ifconfig

tokens.exp: keyword: the next token is the mask
keyword: the next token is the broadcast address
network address with all host bits set to 1

blocks.text: BSD `ifconfig` shows `netmask 0xffffff00`, where Linux shows `/24` or `255.255.255.0`. `netstat -rn` on macOS abbreviates networks in a third way: `192.168.1` drops trailing zero octets and means `192.168.1.0/24`, and a bare `169.254` means `169.254.0.0/16`. A `/N` suffix is printed only when the mask differs from the old classful default, as in `10.8.5/24` or `224.0.0/4`. All of these are the same information in different clothes.
Network, broadcast, first, last, usable
For any prefix length `p`, the host part has `32 - p` bits. From that you get everything:

The "minus 2" removes the network address (it names the network itself) and the broadcast address (packets sent to it reach every host on the segment). Two special cases break the rule. A **/31** has two addresses and no broadcast; RFC 3021 allows both for point-to-point links between routers. A **/32** is a single host, used for loopback addresses and host routes.
The magic-number method
You can do all of this on paper in ten seconds without binary:

items.text: Find the **interesting octet**: the one where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. For /26 that is the fourth (mask 192).
**Block size** = 256 minus the mask octet: 256 - 192 = 64.
List the multiples of the block size in that octet: 0, 64, 128, 192. The address falls in exactly one block: 23 is in `[0, 63]`.
The block's first value is the network (`.0`), the last value is the broadcast (`.63`), everything between is usable.

blocks.text: A harder case where the interesting octet is the third: `10.20.77.130/20`. The mask is `255.255.240.0`, so block size 256 - 240 = 16 in the third octet. Multiples of 16: ..., 64, 80, ... and 77 is in `[64, 79]`. Network `10.20.64.0`, broadcast `10.20.79.255`, usable `10.20.64.1` to `10.20.79.254`, and 2^12 - 2 = 4094 hosts. Everything after the interesting octet is 0 in the network address and 255 in the broadcast.
Type a few addresses into the calculator above and compare the bit bar with your paper answer. Then use the drill generator below until you can get five right in a row without help.
Special and private ranges

Not every address is routable on the public internet. Some blocks are reserved for particular jobs, and recognizing them at a glance is a daily skill: a `169.254` address in `ifconfig` tells you DHCP failed before you run a single test.

head: Block
Name
What it is for
rows: 16.7 million addresses; big organizations and VPNs
`172.16.0.0` to `172.31.255.255`; Docker uses this range by default
your ISP's own private space; also used by Tailscale
self-assigned when DHCP fails; never routed
`0.0.0.0` means "any" or "unspecified"; `0.0.0.0/0` is the default route

blocks.text: **RFC 1918** addresses are free for anyone to use inside their own network and are never routed on the public internet. Your router performs **NAT** (Network Address Translation): it rewrites the private source address of outgoing packets to its single public address and keeps a table so replies find their way back. With CGNAT your ISP does the same trick a second time, which is why a home server behind it cannot accept incoming connections.

The private block is `172.16.0.0` to `172.31.255.255`, sixteen contiguous /16 networks. `172.32.x.x` and `172.15.x.x` are ordinary public addresses. People misremember this and mark real internet hosts as private. With the magic number: second octet mask is 240 (/12), block size 16, so the block starting at 16 ends at 31.

Python's `ipaddress` module knows these categories. Be aware that the exact boundaries of `is_private` and `is_global` have shifted slightly between Python releases as the IANA registries changed, so test the ones you care about:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip
for text in ["10.1.2.3", "8.8.8.8", "127.0.0.1", "169.254.7.7", "224.0.0.251", "172.32.0.1"]:
    a = ip.ip_address(text)
    kinds = [k for k in ("is_private", "is_loopback", "is_link_local", "is_multicast") if getattr(a, k)]
    print(f"{text:<12} {kinds}")

blocks.text: Splitting and joining: VLSM and summarization
**VLSM** (variable-length subnet masks) means giving each segment a block just big enough for it, instead of cutting a network into equal pieces. The method:

items.text: List the segments by size, **largest first**.
For each, find the smallest block with room for the hosts plus two (network and broadcast): the host bits are `ceil(log2(hosts + 2))`.
Hand out blocks from the start of the range, each aligned to its own size. Aligning is automatic when you go largest first.

blocks.text: Plan `10.10.0.0/24` for servers (100 hosts), office (50), labs (25), guests (12) and two router links (2 each):

blocks.code:
import ipaddress

def vlsm(base, needs):
    pool = ipaddress.ip_network(base)
    cursor = int(pool.network_address)
    plan = []
    for name, hosts in sorted(needs.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
        host_bits = (hosts + 1).bit_length()          # smallest bits with 2**bits >= hosts + 2
        net = ipaddress.ip_network((cursor, 32 - host_bits))
        plan.append((name, net, net.num_addresses - 2))
        cursor += net.num_addresses
    return plan

needs = {"servers": 100, "office": 50, "labs": 25, "guests": 12, "link-a": 2, "link-b": 2}
for name, net, usable in vlsm("10.10.0.0/24", needs):
    print(f"{name:<8} {str(net):<16} {usable:>3} usable")
blocks.out:
servers  10.10.0.0/25     126 usable
office   10.10.0.128/26    62 usable
labs     10.10.0.192/27    30 usable
guests   10.10.0.224/28    14 usable
link-a   10.10.0.240/30     2 usable
link-b   10.10.0.244/30     2 usable

blocks.text: The first block, `10.10.0.0/25`, takes the first 128 addresses. Each later block starts where the previous one ended. `10.10.0.248/29` and above remain free for growth. Going smallest-first would leave gaps, because a /25 cannot start at `.64`.

**Summarization** (also called route aggregation or supernetting) is the reverse: replacing several adjacent routes with one. It works only when the blocks are contiguous and the first one is aligned on the combined size. Four /24s starting at `192.168.0.0` collapse into `192.168.0.0/22`: two more bits become host bits, each /24 differs only in those bits.

`192.168.1.0/24` through `192.168.4.0/24` do **not** summarize into one /22, because the run starts at `.1` instead of a multiple of 4. Summarization is how the internet's routing table stays at around a million entries instead of billions.
The routing table and longest-prefix match

Every host has a **routing table**: a list of `destination prefix -> where to send it` entries. For each outgoing packet the kernel finds **every** entry whose prefix contains the destination address and picks the one with the **longest prefix** (most specific). The default route `0.0.0.0/0` matches everything with a prefix of zero bits, so it only wins when nothing else matches.
The same logic in Python, with the `in` operator testing membership of an address in a network:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

table = {
    "0.0.0.0/0":      "default via 192.168.1.1 (en0)",
    "192.168.1.0/24": "direct on en0",
    "10.8.0.0/16":    "via VPN utun4",
    "10.8.5.0/24":    "via VPN utun4, restricted",
    "127.0.0.0/8":    "loopback lo0",
}

def lookup(dest):
    dest = ip.ip_address(dest)
    matches = [ip.ip_network(p) for p in table if dest in ip.ip_network(p)]
    best = max(matches, key=lambda n: n.prefixlen)
    return best, table[str(best)]

for d in ["192.168.1.50", "10.8.5.77", "10.8.200.1", "93.184.216.34", "127.0.0.1"]:
    net, how = lookup(d)
    print(f"{d:<14} -> {str(net):<15} {how}")

blocks.text: If the winning entry is **direct** (the destination is inside a network you are attached to), the host sends the frame straight to the destination's MAC address, found with ARP. Otherwise it sends the frame to the **gateway's** MAC address, and the packet's IP destination stays the same. That is the only job of the default gateway: be the next stop for everything not on the local network.

blocks.name: netstat -rn reading
blocks.sum: Print the kernel routing table numerically so you can see which prefix and gateway each destination uses.

how.text: The kernel keeps a routing table in memory, and `netstat -r` dumps it. `-n` prints numbers instead of trying to resolve names. Each row is one prefix. The **Gateway** column holds the next-hop address, or `link#N` when the network is directly attached (no gateway, deliver locally), or a MAC address for entries that ARP created.

macOS abbreviates the Destination column: `192.168.1` is `192.168.1.0/24`, a bare `127` is `127.0.0.0/8`, and `default` is `0.0.0.0/0`. A bare `169.254` is the link-local block. **Flags** tell you the entry type: `U` up, `G` uses a gateway, `H` is a host route (a /32), `S` was added statically, `C` or `c` generates cloned entries on use, `L` holds link-layer info, `W` was cloned from another route, `I` is tied to one interface, `b` is a broadcast address.

flags.d: Do not resolve addresses to names.
Only IPv4 routes (`-f inet6` for IPv6).

default            192.168.1.1        UGScg             en0
127                127.0.0.1          UCS               lo0
127.0.0.1          127.0.0.1          UH                lo0
169.254            link#14            UCS               en0      !
192.168.1          link#14            UCS               en0      !
192.168.1.1        a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9   UHLWIir           en0   1198

gotchas: When a VPN is connected you may see several `default` rows (some with an `I` flag for interface-scoped). The unscoped one on the first line is the one that wins for ordinary traffic.

blocks.name: route -n get
blocks.sum: Ask the kernel which route, gateway and interface it would use to reach a destination.

how.text: `route get` performs the longest-prefix lookup for you and prints the winning entry: the matching destination and mask, the gateway, the outgoing interface and the interface MTU. It is the quickest way to answer "which way will this packet leave?", and it only reads state. `-n` keeps it from resolving names, and `default` as the destination shows the default route.

examples.desc: Show the default route
examples.out:
route to: default
destination: default
       mask: default
    gateway: 192.168.1.1
  interface: en0
      flags: <UP,GATEWAY,DONE,STATIC,PRCLONING,GLOBAL>

gotchas: With a VPN active, `route -n get 10.8.5.77` shows the tunnel interface (`utun`), while `route -n get 93.184.216.34` shows `en0`. That difference is longest-prefix match at work.

blocks.text: IPv6: the same ideas with 128 bits
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons. Two rules shorten them:

items.text: Leading zeros in a group can be dropped: `0042` becomes `42`.
**One** run of all-zero groups can be replaced by `::`. Only one, otherwise the length would be ambiguous.

blocks.text: `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329` therefore compresses to `2001:db8::ff00:42:8329`. Prefixes work as in CIDR (`2001:db8:1234::/48`), but there is no broadcast and no dotted mask. A normal LAN is a **/64**: 64 bits of network prefix, 64 bits of interface identifier. That is fixed by the way address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) works, so you do not subnet below /64 on ordinary LANs.

head: Prefix
Type
Notes
rows: public, routable; most start with `2` or `3`
every IPv6 interface has one; valid only on the local link, shown as `fe80::1%en0` with a scope
IPv6's RFC 1918: in practice `fd00::/8` with a random 40-bit prefix
replaces broadcast; `ff02::1` is all nodes on the link

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

a = ip.ip_address("2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329")
print(a.compressed)
print(a.exploded)
net = ip.ip_network("2001:db8:1234::/48")
print(net.num_addresses == 2**80, next(net.subnets(new_prefix=64)))
print(ip.ip_address("fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b").is_link_local)

blocks.text: The `%en0` you see after a link-local address on macOS is the **zone ID**: because every interface has an `fe80::` address, the address alone does not say which link to use. When you ping one, include the zone: `ping6 fe80::1%en0`.
MAC addresses, OUIs, EUI-64 and MTU

A **MAC address** is a 48-bit hardware address used on the local link (Ethernet and Wi-Fi), written as six hex octets: `f0:18:98:3a:6d:21`. The first three octets are the **OUI** (Organizationally Unique Identifier) assigned to the manufacturer, so `f0:18:98` identifies Apple in the IEEE registry, and the last three are the device's serial part. Two bits in the first octet carry meaning:

items.text: **Bit 0 (I/G)**: 0 means unicast, 1 means multicast or broadcast. `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff` is the Ethernet broadcast address.

**Bit 1 (U/L)**: 0 means universally administered (burned in by the vendor), 1 means **locally administered** (assigned by software). For a unicast address that means the second hex digit is `2`, `6`, `a` or `e` (`3`, `7`, `b` and `f` are locally administered multicast).

blocks.text: Modern iPhones, Macs and Android phones use a randomized, locally administered MAC per Wi-Fi network ("Private Wi-Fi Address" in Apple's settings) for privacy. The practical effect: the OUI of a phone on your LAN will often not match any vendor, and its MAC may change if you forget and rejoin the network.

blocks.code:
def describe(mac):
    first = int(mac.split(":")[0], 16)
    cast = "multicast/broadcast" if first & 1 else "unicast"
    admin = "locally administered" if first & 2 else "vendor-assigned"
    return f"{mac:<19} {cast}, {admin}"

for m in ["f0:18:98:3a:6d:21", "3a:11:22:33:44:55", "ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff", "01:00:5e:00:00:fb"]:
    print(describe(m))
blocks.out:
f0:18:98:3a:6d:21   unicast, vendor-assigned
3a:11:22:33:44:55   unicast, locally administered
ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff   multicast/broadcast, locally administered
01:00:5e:00:00:fb   multicast/broadcast, vendor-assigned

blocks.text: You can see MACs on your own machine. Note how `arp` prints the bytes without leading zeros, and that the last entry is the Ethernet broadcast address.

blocks.code:
$ ifconfig en0 | grep ether
	ether f0:18:98:3a:6d:21
$ arp -a
router.lan (192.168.1.1) at a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
pi.lan (192.168.1.50) at dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
nas.lan (192.168.1.60) at 0:11:32:aa:3:5d on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
printer.lan (192.168.1.70) at 3c:2a:f4:9:d8:62 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
homeassistant.lan (192.168.1.90) at b8:27:eb:44:19:e0 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
? (192.168.1.255) at ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
$ arp -a | awk '{print $2, $4}'
(192.168.1.1) a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9
(192.168.1.50) dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8
(192.168.1.60) 0:11:32:aa:3:5d
(192.168.1.70) 3c:2a:f4:9:d8:62
(192.168.1.90) b8:27:eb:44:19:e0
(192.168.1.255) ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

blocks.text: EUI-64

Before randomized identifiers, an IPv6 host formed the last 64 bits of its address from its MAC: split the MAC in half, insert `ff:fe` in the middle, and **flip the U/L bit** (XOR the first octet with `0x02`). For `f0:18:98:3a:6d:21` that gives `f218:98ff:fe3a:6d21`, so the link-local address is `fe80::f218:98ff:fe3a:6d21`.

macOS and current Windows and Linux releases default to stable-but-random interface identifiers instead, which is why the `fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b` address on your own Mac has no `ff:fe` in the middle. EUI-64 survives mostly on routers, printers, IoT devices and in older documentation, and when you see `ff:fe` in the middle of an address you can recover the MAC.

blocks.title: macOS drops leading zeros in MACs

blocks.text: `arp -a` on macOS prints `0:11:32:aa:3:5d`, not `00:11:32:aa:03:5d`. If you compare MACs from `arp` against a vendor list or another tool, normalize them first, for example in Python with `":".join(f"{int(x, 16):02x}" for x in mac.split(":"))`.
MTU

The **MTU** (maximum transmission unit) is the largest IP packet a link can carry without fragmenting it: **1500 bytes** on Ethernet and normal Wi-Fi, 1492 on many PPPoE DSL links, up to 9000 on jumbo-frame LANs. Subtract the 20-byte IPv4 header and a 20-byte TCP header and you get the TCP **MSS** of 1460 bytes. For a ping, 1500 - 20 (IP) - 8 (ICMP) leaves 1472 bytes of payload, which is the number you will use in [Reachability and path](#net-reach) to measure a path's real MTU. `ifconfig en0` shows `mtu 1500` in its first line.
Tools for the job
macOS has no subnet calculator built in. Two Homebrew packages fill the gap, and Python's `ipaddress` module (below) is always there.

blocks.name: ipcalc
blocks.sum: Print network, broadcast, host range and binary breakdown for an address and mask.
blocks.syntax: ipcalc address[/prefix] [netmask]   or   ipcalc address/prefix -s size1 size2 ...

how.text: The Homebrew `ipcalc` (a Perl program by Krischan Jodies, version 0.51) takes an address with a prefix or a dotted mask and prints a table: the address and mask in dotted and binary form with the network/host boundary marked by a space, the wildcard, the network, first and last usable host, broadcast and the host count. Given a second mask it also shows the resulting subnets, and with `-s` followed by sizes it performs a VLSM split of the block you give it. Install with `brew install ipcalc`. Use it as a cross-check for your own arithmetic.

blocks.name: sipcalc
blocks.sum: A calculator for IPv4 and IPv6 subnets that prints addresses in decimal, hex and binary.

how.text: `sipcalc` (installed with `brew install sipcalc`) takes one or more addresses and reports the network address, mask in several forms, broadcast, number of addresses and usable range. It handles IPv6 too, including expanded and compressed forms, which `ipcalc` does less well. Run `sipcalc -h` to see the list of options on your version, since they differ between releases.

blocks.name: ifconfig netmask
blocks.sum: Read an interface's address, hex netmask and broadcast address, and convert them to a prefix length.

how.text: `ifconfig en0` prints one block per interface. The `inet` line holds the IPv4 address, `netmask` in hex, and `broadcast`. Convert the hex by counting four bits per `f` and adding the partial digit (`e` 3, `c` 2, `8` 1). The `inet6` lines hold IPv6 addresses with their prefix length (already decimal) and, for link-local, a `%en0` scope. `ether` is the MAC address and `mtu` is in the first line. The deep dive is in [Seeing your own network](#net-local).

examples.desc: Show your IPv4 line
Turn the hex mask into a prefix length

blocks.text: Python's ipaddress module

`ipaddress` is in the standard library and does everything above with checking built in, so it is the right tool once you understand the arithmetic. These blocks run in the page, so edit them and press Run.

`ip_network()` builds a network object. With `strict=True` (the default) it rejects an address that has host bits set, which catches the classic "I typed the host address instead of the network" mistake:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

try:
    ip.ip_network("192.168.1.23/26")
except ValueError as e:
    print("error:", e)

net = ip.ip_network("192.168.1.23/26", strict=False)
print(net)
print(net.network_address, net.broadcast_address)
print(net.netmask, net.hostmask, net.prefixlen)
print(net.num_addresses)

tokens.exp: constructor that parses a CIDR string into a network object
text: an address with a prefix; here it has host bits set
keyword: accept host bits and clear them instead of raising ValueError

blocks.text: `hosts()` yields the usable addresses lazily; it returns an iterator, so wrap it in `list()` only for small networks. `/31` and `/32` follow their special rules:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

net = ip.ip_network("10.10.0.0/28")
hosts = list(net.hosts())
print(len(hosts), hosts[0], hosts[-1])
print(list(ip.ip_network("10.0.0.0/31").hosts()))
print(list(ip.ip_network("10.0.0.7/32").hosts()))

iface = ip.ip_interface("192.168.1.23/24")
print(iface.ip, iface.network, iface.with_netmask)

blocks.text: `subnets()` splits a network, `supernet()` goes up one level, and `collapse_addresses()` merges a list into the fewest networks:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

net = ip.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24")
for sub in net.subnets(prefixlen_diff=2):
    print(sub)
print(list(net.subnets(new_prefix=26))[2].supernet())
nets = [ip.ip_network(f"192.168.{i}.0/24") for i in range(4)]
print(list(ip.collapse_addresses(nets)))
print(list(ip.summarize_address_range(ip.ip_address("10.0.0.5"), ip.ip_address("10.0.0.20"))))

blocks.text: Membership and overlap tests answer "is this host in that network?" and "do these two plans collide?":

blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

lan = ip.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24")
print(ip.ip_address("192.168.1.77") in lan, ip.ip_address("192.168.2.77") in lan)
print(lan.overlaps(ip.ip_network("192.168.1.128/25")))
print(ip.ip_network("192.168.1.128/25").subnet_of(lan))
print(sorted([ip.ip_address(x) for x in ["10.0.0.10", "10.0.0.9", "10.0.0.100"]]))
print(int(ip.ip_address("192.168.1.23")), ip.ip_address(3232235799))

blocks.name: ipaddress.ip_network()
blocks.sum: Build an IPv4 or IPv6 network object from a CIDR string.

how.text: The constructor parses the text, detects IPv4 or IPv6, splits address and prefix and stores them as integers. Because networks are integers internally, `in`, `overlaps()`, sorting and `subnets()` are cheap arithmetic rather than string handling. A mask can be given as a prefix (`/26`) or dotted (`/255.255.255.192`).

examples.desc: Normalize a network that was written with a host address
examples.code:
import ipaddress
n = ipaddress.ip_network("172.16.45.200/20", strict=False)
print(n, n.netmask, n.num_addresses)

gotchas: `strict=True` raises `ValueError: ... has host bits set` for `192.168.1.23/24`. Use `ip_interface()` when you want to keep the host address and also get its network.

blocks.name: ipaddress.ip_address()
blocks.sum: Build an IPv4 or IPv6 address object that supports comparison, arithmetic and category tests.

how.text: An address object wraps a single integer. That is why you can compare and sort addresses numerically, add an integer to move along the address space, and convert with `int()` and back. Properties such as `is_private`, `is_loopback`, `is_link_local` and `is_multicast` test the address against the reserved blocks from this chapter.

examples.desc: Compare, add and test addresses
examples.code:
import ipaddress
a = ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.23")
print(a + 5, a.is_private, a in ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24"))

notes: Adding an integer moves along the address space; subtracting two addresses gives an integer distance.

blocks.name: ipaddress.ip_interface()
blocks.sum: Hold a host address together with its network, the way `ifconfig` shows it.

how.text: An interface object keeps what a network configuration really holds: *this host* address plus *its* network. `.ip` gives the host, `.network` the containing network with host bits cleared, and `.netmask` the mask. This mirrors one `inet` line of `ifconfig`.

examples.desc: Split an address-with-prefix into its parts
examples.code:
import ipaddress
i = ipaddress.ip_interface("192.168.1.23/26")
print(i.ip, i.network, i.netmask)

blocks.name: net.subnets()
blocks.sum: Yield the smaller networks that make up a network, by prefix difference or new prefix length.

how.text: Splitting a network is arithmetic on the prefix length: a `/24` with `new_prefix=26` becomes four consecutive /26 blocks, each starting at a multiple of 64 in the last octet. The method yields them lazily in address order, so splitting a /8 into /24s does not build a huge list unless you ask for one.

examples.desc: Cut a /24 into four /26 blocks
examples.code:
import ipaddress
print([str(n) for n in ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.0.0/24").subnets(new_prefix=26)])

notes: Only one of `prefixlen_diff` and `new_prefix` may be given. `net.supernet()` is the inverse and returns the enclosing network one bit shorter.

blocks.name: ipaddress.collapse_addresses()
blocks.sum: Merge a list of networks into the smallest equivalent list, joining adjacent ones.

how.text: The function sorts the networks, drops any that are contained in another, and repeatedly merges pairs of sibling blocks that together form a block one bit shorter. This is route summarization: it succeeds only for contiguous, correctly aligned blocks, which is why `192.168.1.0/24` and `192.168.2.0/24` stay separate.

examples.desc: Summarize contiguous and non-contiguous blocks
examples.code:
import ipaddress as ip
nets = [ip.ip_network(n) for n in ("10.0.0.0/24", "10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24")]
print([str(n) for n in ip.collapse_addresses(nets)])

notes: Networks must all be the same IP version. The result is sorted.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Counting the network and broadcast addresses as hosts.** A /24 has 256 addresses and 254 usable hosts, a /30 has 4 and 2.
**Subnetting on the wrong octet.** Find the octet where the mask is not 0 or 255 first; only that octet needs maths.

**Assuming a block starts wherever you like.** A /26 block must start at a multiple of 64 in its octet, a /20 at a multiple of 16 in the third octet. `192.168.1.40/26` is a host inside `192.168.1.0/26`, not a network.
**Forgetting 172.16.0.0/12 is only 16 to 31 in the second octet.**
**Reading `0xffffff00` as 255.255.255.0 without checking.** It is, but `0xfffffc00` is 255.255.252.0 (a /22), and mixing the two up on an address plan costs hours.
**Treating MAC or IPv6 text as fixed width.** macOS prints `0:11:32:aa:3:5d`; IPv6 compresses zero groups. Normalize with `ipaddress` or `f"{x:02x}"` before comparing strings.

Do the paper problems with the magic-number method before you let Python check them. The check in the first exercise computes the right answers from `ipaddress`, so you can submit as often as you like.

blocks.title: Ten subnetting problems

task.text: Fill in the dictionary `answers` with a string for each problem. Work them out by hand first (magic-number method), then submit to see which ones are wrong.

items.text: Network address of `192.168.1.77/24`
Broadcast address of `10.1.2.3/8`
Number of usable hosts in a `/27`
`ifconfig` shows `netmask 0xfffffc00`. What is the prefix length? (answer like `22`)
Network address of `172.16.45.200/20`
Broadcast address of `192.168.5.130/26`
Dotted-decimal mask for a `/19`
The longest prefix (largest number, answer like `/24`) that still fits 500 hosts
Is `10.4.9.255/22` a `network`, `broadcast` or `host` address?
The one CIDR block that summarizes `192.168.8.0/24` through `192.168.11.0/24`

hints: For 5 and 6 find the block size first: a /20 has block 16 in the third octet, a /26 has block 64 in the fourth.
For 8, 2^9 = 512 addresses give 510 usable hosts, which fits 500. How many host bits is that?
For 9, a /22 has block size 4 in the third octet, so the block containing 9 runs from 8 to 11. Is 9.255 the last address?

why.text: Each answer follows from three steps: count host bits (32 minus prefix), find the block size in the interesting octet, locate the block that holds the address. Problem 4 is why you learn the hex form: `fffffc00` is 16 + 6 = 22 ones. Problem 9 is the trap: ending in `.255` does not make an address a broadcast unless every host bit is 1, and with a /22 only `10.4.11.255` qualifies.

blocks.check:
import ipaddress as ip
expected = {
    1: str(ip.ip_network("192.168.1.77/24", strict=False).network_address),
    2: str(ip.ip_network("10.1.2.3/8", strict=False).broadcast_address),
    3: str(ip.ip_network("10.0.0.0/27").num_addresses - 2),
    4: str(ip.ip_network("0.0.0.0/255.255.252.0").prefixlen),
    5: str(ip.ip_network("172.16.45.200/20", strict=False).network_address),
    6: str(ip.ip_network("192.168.5.130/26", strict=False).broadcast_address),
    7: str(ip.ip_network("0.0.0.0/19").netmask),
    8: "/23",
    9: "host",
    10: "192.168.8.0/22",
}
for k, v in expected.items():
    got = str(answers.get(k, "")).strip()
    assert got == v, f"Problem {k}: '{got}' is not right. Recheck the block size for that prefix."

blocks.title: Summarize four /24s

task.text: Write `summarize(cidrs)` that takes a list of CIDR strings and returns the shortest list of CIDR strings (as text, sorted) that covers exactly the same addresses. Use only what you learned in this chapter.

hints: The standard library already has a function that merges networks.
`ipaddress.collapse_addresses` takes network objects and returns an iterator of network objects.
blocks.solution:
import ipaddress

def summarize(cidrs):
    nets = [ipaddress.ip_network(c) for c in cidrs]
    return [str(n) for n in ipaddress.collapse_addresses(nets)]

why.text: The third assertion is the interesting one: `192.168.1.0` and `192.168.2.0` are adjacent but a /23 must start at an even third octet, so they cannot merge. Alignment, not adjacency alone, decides.

blocks.title: A VLSM plan for five departments

task.text: Divide `172.16.4.0/23` among five departments, largest first, starting at the beginning of the range: Engineering needs 200 hosts, Operations 90, Sales 45, Support 20, Guests 6. Fill the dictionary `plan` with each department's network in CIDR notation, working it out by hand.

hints: Host bits needed: 200 hosts + 2 = 202 addresses, so 2^8 = 256 (a /24). Repeat for each department.
After the /24 at `172.16.4.0`, the next free address is `172.16.5.0`. A /25 takes 128 addresses, so the next one starts at `172.16.5.128`.

why.text: Largest first keeps every block aligned: 256, then 128, 64, 32 and 8 addresses each start at a multiple of their own size. The leftover `172.16.5.232` upward (24 addresses) is room to grow. The `vlsm()` function earlier in this chapter produces the same plan.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose, then fix it

task.text: This code crashes with `ValueError: ... has host bits set`. Fix it **without changing the string** so that `net` is the network that contains the host, and `host_count` is the number of usable addresses.

hints: Read the error: the constructor refuses addresses with bits set in the host part.
The constructor has a keyword argument that relaxes this check.
blocks.solution:
import ipaddress

net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.23/26", strict=False)
host_count = net.num_addresses - 2

why.text: `strict=True` is a feature. It stops you from silently treating a host address as a network. Pass `strict=False` only when you mean "give me the network that contains this host", or use `ip_interface()` to keep both.

blocks.title: Read your own network

task.text: On your Mac, find your interface's address and hex netmask with `ifconfig`, convert the mask to a prefix length by hand, then confirm with `brew install ipcalc` (or the `subnet` widget above). Write down: network address, broadcast, first and last usable host, number of hosts. Finally run `netstat -rn -f inet | head` and identify which line is your default route and which line is your own network.

hints: `ifconfig en0 | grep 'inet '` (use your interface name if it is not en0; `route -n get default | grep interface` tells you which).
Convert the mask digit by digit: each `f` is 4 ones.
blocks.solution:
ifconfig en0 | grep 'inet '
ipcalc 192.168.1.23/24
netstat -rn -f inet | head

why.text: The `default` row's Gateway is your router; the row whose Destination looks like `192.168.1` with a `link#` gateway is the directly attached network. Every packet to an address inside that prefix skips the router.

blocks.title: Which route wins?
hints: Collect every route whose prefix contains the destination, then take the longest prefix.

why.text: Specificity beats order and beats size. The /24 inside the /16 inside the /8 all match `10.20.30.40`, and the /24 wins. The default route matches everything and only wins when nothing longer matches.

questions.q: A host has 192.168.1.130/26. What are the network and broadcast addresses?
questions.why: A /26 has block size 64, so blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. 130 falls in the block 128 to 191. The last choice lists the first and last usable hosts, not the network and broadcast.

questions.q: macOS `ifconfig` shows `netmask 0xfffffff0`. What prefix length is that?
questions.why: `0xfffffff0` is seven `f`s (28 bits) plus a final `0`, so 28 ones: /28, 16 addresses, 14 usable hosts.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT an RFC 1918 private address?
questions.why: The 172 private block is only 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 (/12). 172.32.0.9 is a public address.

questions.q: A route table has 0.0.0.0/0, 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16. Which entry is used for 10.1.2.3?

options.text: 10.0.0.0/8, because it has the larger block

questions.why: Every entry matches. The kernel picks the most specific one, the one with the longest prefix.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /29 give?
questions.why: A /29 has 3 host bits, 8 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses leaves 6.

questions.q: In `fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b%en0`, what does the `%en0` part tell you?

options.text: The zone (interface) the link-local address belongs to
That the address is a ULA

questions.why: Link-local addresses are only meaningful on one link, and a host with several interfaces has an `fe80::` address on each, so the scope is added after a percent sign.

blocks.text: You will write the same calculator twice: once with pure integer maths, so you prove you understand the bit operations, and once with `ipaddress`, so you have a reference to test against. Then you wrap it in a command-line tool that you can run on your own Mac as `./ipcalc.py 192.168.1.23/26`. Create the file in PyCharm (right-click your project, New, Python File) or with `nano ipcalc.py`.
Step 1: The pure-maths core
These functions turn dotted decimal into a 32-bit integer and back, build a mask from a prefix, and recover a prefix from a mask while rejecting masks that are not a run of 1s followed by 0s.
Step 2: The reference version with ipaddress
Append a second function to the same file that gets the same fields from the standard library. Having two independent implementations is what lets you trust either one.

blocks.code:
def calc_lib(address, prefix):
    net = ipaddress.ip_network(f"{address}/{prefix}", strict=False)
    if prefix >= 31:
        hosts = list(net.hosts())
        first, last, usable = hosts[0], hosts[-1], net.num_addresses
    else:
        first, last, usable = net.network_address + 1, net.broadcast_address - 1, net.num_addresses - 2
    return {
        "address": address,
        "prefix": prefix,
        "netmask": str(net.netmask),
        "netmask_hex": f"0x{int(net.netmask):08x}",
        "wildcard": str(net.hostmask),
        "network": str(net.network_address),
        "broadcast": str(net.broadcast_address),
        "first": str(first),
        "last": str(last),
        "usable": usable,
    }

blocks.text: Step 3: Prove they agree

This block pastes the pure-maths functions and checks them against `ipaddress` for 2,000 random addresses at random prefixes. Press Run. If you change a function above and it stops agreeing, this is the test that tells you.

blocks.code:
import ipaddress, random

FULL = 0xFFFFFFFF
def to_dotted(n): return ".".join(str((n >> s) & 255) for s in (24, 16, 8, 0))
def mask_from_prefix(p): return (FULL << (32 - p)) & FULL

def network_math(ip_int, prefix):
    mask = mask_from_prefix(prefix)
    return to_dotted(ip_int & mask), to_dotted(ip_int & mask | (~mask & FULL))

random.seed(7)
checked = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    ip_int = random.getrandbits(32)
    prefix = random.randint(0, 32)
    net = ipaddress.ip_network((ip_int, prefix), strict=False)
    assert network_math(ip_int, prefix) == (str(net.network_address), str(net.broadcast_address)), (ip_int, prefix)
    checked += 1
print("all", checked, "cases agree")

blocks.text: Step 4: The command-line wrapper
Append the output and argument-parsing code to the end of `ipcalc.py`.
Make it executable and try the four input spellings. The two engines must print identical output:

blocks.code:
chmod +x ipcalc.py
./ipcalc.py 192.168.1.23/26
./ipcalc.py 192.168.1.23/255.255.255.192
./ipcalc.py 192.168.1.23/0xffffffc0
diff <(./ipcalc.py 10.20.77.130/20) <(./ipcalc.py 10.20.77.130/20 --lib) && echo engines agree
./ipcalc.py 10.0.0.1/255.0.255.0; echo "exit status $?"

blocks.text: The last command feeds a mask whose 1s are not contiguous, so the program should print an error on stderr and exit with status 2.

Print the binary form of the address with the network/host boundary marked by a space, like `ipcalc` does. Accept `--split N` to list the subnets of the block when cut into N equal parts. Add IPv6 support by swapping `to_int` for `ipaddress.ip_address` and replacing 32 with 128. Feed it your own `ifconfig` line: `./ipcalc.py $(ifconfig en0 | awk '/inet /{print $2 "/" $4}')`.

terms.def: Classless Inter-Domain Routing: writing a network as address/prefix-length, where the prefix can be any number of bits
An 8-bit group; the four numbers in a dotted IPv4 address
32-bit value of leading ones and trailing zeros that separates the network part of an address from the host part
The number of leading one-bits in a mask, written after a slash (/24)
The inverted subnet mask (0s where the mask has 1s); used in router access lists and OSPF
The address with every host bit set to 1; delivered to every host on the segment
Variable-Length Subnet Masking: carving a block into subnets of different sizes
Replacing several contiguous routes by one shorter-prefix route (also called aggregation or supernetting)
The routing rule: of all entries that contain the destination, use the one with the most specific (longest) prefix
The standard that reserves 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16 for private networks
Network Address Translation: rewriting private addresses to a public one at the router and tracking the mapping
Carrier-grade NAT: an ISP-level NAT using 100.64.0.0/10, so customers share public addresses
An address valid only on one network segment: 169.254.0.0/16 for IPv4, fe80::/10 for IPv6
Organizationally Unique Identifier: the first three octets of a MAC address, assigned to a manufacturer
A way to build a 64-bit IPv6 interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC by inserting ff:fe and flipping one bit
Maximum Transmission Unit: the largest packet a link carries without fragmenting (1500 bytes on Ethernet)
